analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare drug plans to disclose when pharmacy benefit manager committees overrule clinical recommendations on which drugs are covered.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one Republican cosponsor, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Medicare Part D rules so that drug plan sponsors must report to Medicare any committee or individual affiliated with the plan or its pharmacy benefit manager that can overrule the plan's pharmacy and therapeutic committee — the clinical panel that recommends which drugs are covered and how. For each override, plans would have to identify the drugs affected and explain why. It would also order a Government Accountability Office study of these shadow committees and their effect on patients' access to drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries would gain visibility into who really decides which drugs their plans cover. When a PBM-affiliated committee overrules a clinical recommendation — for example, to favor a drug with a bigger rebate — patients and their doctors currently have no way to see it. Mandatory disclosure of those overrides and their justifications, plus a GAO study of how often they happen and how tools like prior authorization affect access, would give regulators and the public evidence to act on.

how_it_helps.text: It requires Medicare drug plans to tell CMS the names, roles, and composition of any affiliated committee or individual that can overrule the pharmacy and therapeutic committee on which drugs are covered.
Plans must disclose every drug whose coverage was changed by such an affiliated committee, with a written justification for each decision.

It directs the Government Accountability Office to study how often these overrides happen, trends in utilization-management tools like prior authorization and step therapy, and their impact on beneficiary access to drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare drug plan sponsors and their pharmacy benefit managers would bear the cost of new reporting requirements, having to document and justify every formulary decision that departs from the clinical panel's recommendation. If disclosure reveals conflicts of interest, PBMs could face pressure on a business model built on hidden formulary leverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: The bill requires disclosure only — it does not prohibit PBMs from overriding clinical recommendations or cap what they can charge, so the conflicts of interest it exposes could continue legally.
The reporting burden falls on Medicare drug plan sponsors and their pharmacy benefit managers, and the GAO study was not due until January 2029, meaning no new public findings would emerge for years.
It applies only to standalone prescription drug plans, leaving formulary decision-making in Medicare Advantage drug plans outside the new reporting requirement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is modest and low-cost: it imposes reporting paperwork on plan sponsors and PBMs but gives Medicare officials and the public a clearer window into who actually decides which drugs are covered. Its main drawback is that transparency is not enforcement — it names and documents conflicts of interest without banning them, and the required GAO report would not arrive until 2029, so patients would gain information long before any potential fix. It is a reasonable first step rather than a remedy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat with no further action through the end of the Congress.

narrative.text: Senator Carper introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, joined by Senator Grassley, giving it one Republican cosponsor in addition to its Democratic sponsor.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No committee vote, floor action, or further step ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and the insurers that contract with them benefit, since no disclosure requirement on their formulary decisions was ever enacted from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pharmacy benefit managers and Part D insurers

for.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 20, 2023 and sent it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it a bipartisan two-senate effort.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 20, 2023 and took no further action on it, never marking it up or advancing it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — and its failure came from committee inaction rather than a recorded party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would force PBMs and the plans they contract with to disclose every time an affiliated committee overrules the clinical panel on drug coverage decisions, exposing a practice that can steer patients toward drugs the PBM profits from. PBMs' interest in keeping these decisions hidden runs against patients' interest in affordable, clinically sound coverage.
Insurers offering standalone Part D plans would take on new reporting duties, but the bill mainly targets their PBM partners' hidden role; the added compliance cost is real but modest.

Beneficiaries and the pharmacies that serve them would benefit if hidden formulary overrides — which can push patients onto costlier or less suitable drugs — are documented and eventually curbed. The GAO study explicitly examines how these tools affect beneficiary access.
